# Introduction

# Background

## Data Sources

- This data comes directly from the findings of Cortez and Silva (2008). Looking at data from two Portuguese secondary schools, they show how grades in Mathematics and Portuguese differ based on levels of studying. They separate studying levels into 5 categories (1 being the "very good", 5 being the "insufficient"). They include many other regressors and controls in their data set, including age, sex, parent's education, extracurricular activities, health, and more. 

## Variables
Below are descriptions of the variables we will be using in our analysis:
- studytime: Separated into 5 binary categories. 1 is the best level of studying, 5 is the worst. 
- G3: Final grade, leveled 0-20

Step 1: Fix what the TA asked for
The TA asked us to check group sizes and also compare category 1 against category 4. Do this first, because it changes what goes in the report.
[ ] Count students in each study-time category (1, 2, 3, 4). Put this table in the report. Category 4 (more than 10 hours a week) is probably small, about 35 students. Confirm the real number.
[ ] Keep our main test: lower (1+2) vs. higher (3+4), Welch two-sample t-test.
[ ] Add a second test: category 1 vs. category 4 only, also a Welch t-test. These are the two extremes.
[ ] Say the small group is less stable. If category 4 is small, mention in the Discussion that the 1 vs. 4 result is less reliable.
[ ] Check for final grades of 0. A G3 of 0 usually means the student dropped out, not that they scored zero. Count them, decide as a group whether to keep them, and explain the choice in Background.
Code to start with:
# how many students in each category
por_clean %>% count(studytime)

# how many final grades of 0
por_clean %>% filter(G3 == 0) %>% count(study_group)

# main test: lower vs higher
t.test(G3 ~ study_group, data = por_clean)

# second test: category 1 vs category 4
extremes <- por_clean %>% filter(studytime %in% c(1, 4))
t.test(G3 ~ studytime, data = extremes)
t.test() runs the Welch version by default, so we get the p-value and 95% confidence interval from the same output.
Step 2: Raw data and cleaning file
The cleaning file is a separate .Rmd from the report. It reads the raw file, keeps only what we use, and saves a clean copy that the report reads.
[ ] Put the original student-por.csv in the repo, untouched.
[ ] Make cleaning.Rmd that keeps only studytime and G3, adds the lower/higher group, and saves por_clean.csv.
[ ] Knit it once to make sure it runs.
Watch out: the UCI file is separated by semicolons, not commas, so read_csv() will put everything in one column. Use read_delim().
library(tidyverse)

por <- read_delim("student-por.csv", delim = ";")

por_clean <- por %>%
  select(studytime, G3) %>%
  mutate(study_group = case_when(
    studytime %in% c(1, 2) ~ "Lower",
    studytime %in% c(3, 4) ~ "Higher"
  ))

write_csv(por_clean, "por_clean.csv")


If we decide to drop the G3 = 0 students, add filter(G3 > 0) here and say so in the report.
Step 3: Write the report
Write it for someone who knows nothing about statistics. Statistical terms go only in the Statistical Analysis section.
Introduction
[ ] Opening sentence or two on why this matters to the reader (how much study time actually pays off).
[ ] Our question, stated clearly.
[ ] Thesis: one sentence on what we found. Write it after running the tests. No words like p-value, test or confidence interval.
Background
[ ] Data source with link: UCI Student Performance dataset, collected by Paulo Cortez and Alice Silva from school reports and questionnaires at two Portuguese secondary schools.
[ ] One row = one student's record in the Portuguese course. 649 students total.
[ ] Explain studytime (self-reported weekly hours, categories 1 to 4) and G3 (final grade, 0 to 20 scale).
[ ] Unusual factors: the G3 = 0 students, the small category 4, and that study time is self-reported.
[ ] Graph: side-by-side boxplots of final grade for Lower vs. Higher, with a dot for each group's mean. Explain in 1 to 2 sentences what it shows.
[ ] Small table: number of students and mean final grade per group.
Statistical Analysis
[ ] Define the parameters: μ_H and μ_L = population mean final grade for higher and lower study-time students.
[ ] Name the method: Welch two-sample t-test.
[ ] Check assumptions: independent students, large enough samples or roughly normal grades, and note category 4's small size.
[ ] Hypotheses: H0: μ_H − μ_L = 0 vs. HA: μ_H − μ_L ≠ 0.
[ ] Report the p-value and 95% confidence interval for the main test and the 1 vs. 4 test.
[ ] No interpretation here. Save it for the Discussion.
Discussion
[ ] Explain the results in plain words (for example: "students who study more score about X points higher out of 20").
[ ] Say this is an association, not proof that studying causes higher grades, since students chose how much to study.
[ ] Weaknesses: self-reported study time, only two schools, small category 4, the zeros.
[ ] One or two ideas for future research.
Formatting
[ ] Every chunk uses echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE.
[ ] No code, warnings or printed dataset in the HTML.
[ ] Proofread for grammar. We can be graded on it.
